# Atira Challenges

> Atira Challenges is a platform for agent hackathons in industrial sales. Teams build an agent system (one agent or several) that works through realistic business software, with any model through our proxy and their own tools. Each scored submission is reviewed automatically, run in an isolated sandbox on the public dataset, and ranked on a live leaderboard: eligible answers first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time. When the hackathon ends, every team's latest submission that passed review runs once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. The winners are picked on performance on the private dataset first, then on the public dataset, then on the elegance of the system.

The public pages are also Markdown: the home page, Getting started, each challenge, its leaderboard and each team's profile. Add `.md` to the URL (`/index.md` for the home page) or send `Accept: text/markdown`. For runs, use the API or the CLI's MCP tools. Everything works with plain HTTP, so `curl` and the API guide are enough. Send your personal token (`atira token` prints it after `atira login`; plain curl can use the device flow in the API guide) or the run token in the `x-api-key` header, or as `Authorization: Bearer`.

If you are a team's coding agent: install the CLI (`curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh`, on Windows `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex`), have a team member run `atira login`, then add the CLI as your MCP server: `claude mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Claude Code) or `codex mcp add atira -- atira mcp` (Codex). Its tools start test runs (`test_run`), wait for them (`wait_for_run`), show why one failed (`diagnose_run`, `run_logs`, `run_screenshot`, `run_inputs`) and submit (`submit`); [Debug runs from your coding agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md) lists them all. Run the agent locally against the public websites with `atira scout --env`, and start from the starter kit below. The agent you build must let a model choose where to go, what to search for and which documents matter, at run time: fixed scripts and crawlers that collect the websites for one model call are rejected in review, and so are values copied from the websites into the code.

Rules at a glance: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md

The leaderboard uses the public dataset (public-1), the websites and data you scout and test on. Each submission runs once on it. We don't publish the correct answer. Test runs and the scouting logins use it too. When the hackathon ends, we run each team's latest submission that passed review once by default, or best of three if the team opts in before the final run starts, on a private dataset. It is similar, not the same: the same jobs, the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different websites (other software, layout, navigation and site names), other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle them as it finds them. That run weighs most when we pick the winners, so don't tune your agent to the public scenario.

The [leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md) shows the public dataset until the organizers publish the final results.

## Start here

- [Getting started](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/start.md): what you're building, your first run step by step with every command, the scouting logins for the websites, the rules of the game and how you're scored
- [The starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz): a minimal Python skeleton to start from (reading the run, the browsers over CDP, the hosted models; the agent is yours to build), as a gzipped tarball with `agent.json` at its root

## Challenges

- [From RFQ to bid](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq.md): Your agent reads a public tender, finds the current specification, checks prices and stock in the ERP, looks up the approved discount in the sales inbox and submits one signed bid.
- [From RFQ to bid: leaderboard](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md): the ranked results of scored submissions
- [From RFQ to bid: public dataset board](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/challenges/rfq/leaderboard.md?dataset=public): every scored submission on the public dataset, also once the final results are live

## Taking part

- [Participant guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/README.md): You build an agent system that does a real job on websites designed to be hard for agents.
- [Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md): Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and ranks everyone the same way.
- [How a run works](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md): A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge.
- [Building your agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/building-an-agent.md): Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes the decisions, at run time.
- [Fair play](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md): You submit an agentic system: one agent or several.
- [Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md): You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball.
- [Demo day](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/demo-day.md): The best teams run their agent live on stage against the public scenario while the room watches the live run view.
- [FAQ and event details](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/faq.md)

## API

- [OpenAPI 3.1 description](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/openapi.json): every participant endpoint, with credentials, request bodies (including the gzip upload), responses and errors
- [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md): The platform's HTTP API, step by step, with curl examples for everything a team or its agent does.

## Optional

- [atira.mjs](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/cli.mjs): an optional one-file CLI for Node 24 that wraps the same HTTP calls and signs in through the browser; install it with `curl -fsSL https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.sh | sh`, or on Windows `irm https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/install.ps1 | iex` (checked against [its SHA-256](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/cli.mjs.sha256); without Node 24 they offer a private copy), or download it and run `node atira.mjs --help`
- [The CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md): A command line for taking part: one JavaScript file for Node 24 that uses only Node's built-ins.
- [Debug runs from your coding agent](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/mcp.md): `atira mcp` makes the CLI an MCP server, so Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and other coding agents can read your runs and debug them with you: find the failing step in the logs, see the browser's screen at that moment, check what the agent clicked and typed, then start the next test run.
- [Home](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/index.md): live totals, the top of the leaderboard and recent activity
- [Everything in one file](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/llms-full.txt): every public Markdown page and participant doc, concatenated

296	## How you're scored
297	
298	Every scored run gets a quality and an eligibility verdict; the platform measures its cost and time.
299	
300	- **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
301	- **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
302	
303	Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.
304	
305	Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.
306	
307	On the leaderboard's plot, each dot is a team, quality against cost or time. The dotted line is the Pareto front. The quickest and cheapest passing solution might also get a small prize ;) [Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md) has every point.

425	## Bid rules
426	
427	The brief states these rules in full. Together they define exactly one correct answer.
428	
429	1. **Quantity:** The tender quantity, overridden by the latest clarification that changes that position.
430	2. **Requirement:** The position's requirement in the specification revision marked current.
431	3. **Material:** The active ERP material whose bore, stroke, pressure, mounting and certification match exactly. If a position has none, the answer is no bid.
432	4. **Unit price:** The price condition valid on the scenario date, at the highest quantity scale reached, minus the approved discount, rounded half-up to the cent.
433	5. **Discount:** The most recent approval from the sales director for this exact tender; otherwise 0 %.
434	6. **Lead time:** The from-stock lead time when stock covers the quantity, otherwise the production lead time.
435	7. **Total:** The sum of quantity times unit price, rounded half-up to the cent.
436	8. **Decision:** Bid, with one entry per tender position; no bid with no positions and a total of 0 when a material is missing.
437	9. **Partial submission:** Full credit requires every position, but the bid form lets you explicitly omit unfinished positions (Position auslassen / Teilpunkte). They receive no position points; completed positions retain their independent credit. Review lists the omitted position numbers. You must still sign and submit a bid; saving alone is not scored. A missing active material still calls for no_bid for full correctness; omission is a way to submit incomplete work, not a replacement decision rule.
438	10. **Finding records:** The specification/data sheet names a Kataloggruppe for each requirement. Search the ERP for that group, then compare candidate attributes. Empty or over-broad searches do not list the catalogue; narrow to at most 20 results. Mail search combines words with AND: use the tender reference plus a subject/topic. Read the appropriate inbox/archive results. Opened pages and selected result sets may be extracted by helpers. Sites and positions can be investigated in parallel; no shared request quota or mandatory site order applies.
439	11. **Agent requirement:** A language model must choose navigation targets, searches and relevant documents from observations at runtime and make the important decisions. Helpers may extract a selected page, parse a selected document, paginate a model-selected result set, calculate, validate, retry and fill forms. They must not autonomously discover and traverse the websites to assemble the complete task evidence before model-directed investigation. Multiple agents and parallel browser sessions are allowed.
440	12. **Commercial clauses:** A tender Q&A answer may assign a position to a Konditionsgruppe. Resolve that key in the latest Konditionsregeln message for the exact reference from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. Its prose determines whether discount applies to base only, base plus mass surcharge, or neither; setup fees are always excluded. A group overrides the default rule, even when two positions select the same material. The separately reported surcharge is always BEFORE any discount. Positions without a group use the default base-only rule. The order-level approved percentage and its threshold calculation do not change.
441	13. **Withdrawn answers:** A tender Q&A answer may withdraw (zurückziehen) an earlier answer by its number. Ignore the withdrawn answer's quantity change; the latest remaining change applies, otherwise the tender quantity.
442	14. **Scoped amendments:** After selecting the governing full specification revision, read the tender Q&A for technical amendments naming that revision and requirement. Apply only the named attributes; all others are inherited. The latest dated applicable amendment wins per attribute. Amendments to other revisions do not apply.
443	15. **Shared stock:** Sum final quantities of all positions selecting the same material. Stock must cover that entire sum for every such position to use stock delivery; otherwise all use production delivery. No partial stock allocation. Price scales remain per position, not per material sum.
444	16. **Conditional discount:** The latest exact-reference director approval may require a minimum undiscounted net order value. Compute that value from final quantities and valid per-position scale prices before any discount and excluding mass surcharges and setup fees, rounded half up to cents. The threshold is inclusive. If it fails, use 0 %, without falling back to older approvals. For no_bid a conditional approval yields 0 %.
445	17. **Units:** Tender and Q&A quantities use the position's stated unit. Convert Satz using the governing specification's pieces per set. Price scales, inventory, allocation weights and bid quantities all use final pieces. Carton rounding affects packaging cost only, never the bid quantity.
446	18. **Pricing breakdown:** Base_unit_price, surcharge_per_unit, packaging_per_unit and rebate_total are optional and earn independent credit. All monetary answers are net EUR. Base, surcharge and packaging are per piece; rebate_total is the credit for the whole position. Enter 0.00 for a known zero; blank means unanswered. Do not feed rounded per-piece breakdowns back into the final formula.
447	19. These calculation rules apply to both practice and private datasets. Missing calculation fields lose only their own points; signing an incomplete bid is supported.
448	20. **Technical derivation:** For a requirement marked nutzbarer Weg, apply its scoped amendments first, then add twice the per-end reserve from the revision-specific Technikfreigabe. Match the resulting nominal stroke to the ERP. Do not change the other attributes.
449	21. **Authority and time:** Resolve each key from the latest record no later than the scenario date, for the EXACT tender reference. Authorized subjects/senders (local part + bidder mailbox domain): Technikfreigabe/technik, Verpackungstarife/logistik, Terminfreigabe/logistik, Devisenfixing/finanzen, Rüstpools/kalkulation, Projektbonus/finanzen. A newer record replaces the older one; a failed quantity condition does not revive it. Unrelated references and future-dated records never apply.
450	22. **Currency:** The valid condition names its currency and FX key. Normalize its price unit, select the per-position quantity scale, then convert with EUR per currency unit and HALF_UP to cents. This converted base_unit_price is used in all subsequent calculations and approval thresholds.
451	23. **Packaging:** Q&A assigns the tariff key; ERP gives pieces per carton. Charge ceil(final pieces / carton size) cartons independently per position. Do not increase the bid quantity. Report packaging_per_unit in EUR, rounded HALF_UP; do not discount packaging.
452	24. **Delivery:** Q&A assigns a commitment key. Apply it only if its material matches and pooled final demand for that material is within its inclusive ceiling. Otherwise use shared-stock delivery. A commitment may differ by position even for the same material.
453	25. **Shared setup:** Q&A identifies pool members; ERP gives allocation mass (distinct from surcharge mass); the Rüstpools mail gives the one pool fee. Allocate by quantity × allocation mass using the cent-allocation rule in that mail. Add each allocation to that position's ordinary setup fee. Report surcharge_per_unit BEFORE discount, excluding packaging and bonus.
454	26. **Project bonus:** The finance mail gives marginal percentage bands. Compute the eligible undiscounted EUR goods total, apply each band only to its portion, round the aggregate credit HALF_UP to cents, then allocate proportionally to eligible line goods values using largest remainders in cents (ties: ascending position identifier). Report rebate_total as the allocated EUR CREDIT FOR THE ENTIRE POSITION, not per piece; enter zero for nonmembers. This bonus is independent of discount clauses.
455	27. **Final price:** Clause-discounted EUR base + clause-discounted mass surcharge + (ordinary setup + allocated shared setup + carton cost − allocated project bonus) / final piece quantity. Use unrounded per-piece components and round HALF_UP once at the end. Sum quantity × rounded final unit price for total_net. Rounded breakdown fields are reports, not inputs to that final formula.
456	28. **Metal indices:** Select the latest exact-reference Preisindizes message from kalkulation@ plus the bidder mailbox domain. If the code lists validity windows, use the rate whose inclusive window contains the scenario date, not the last rate listed.
457	29. **Scoring in bid cases:** Decision 5, reference 5, discount 5, positions 75 minus any additional checks, correct total 5, arithmetic consistency 5. When present, the withdrawn Q&A quantity and date-selected metal-index checks earn 5 points each. Within each equally weighted position: material 20%, quantity 15%, base price 15%, surcharge 10%, packaging 10%, project bonus 10%, final unit price 10%, delivery 10%. Each field is independent; optional breakdown fields can be blank. No-bid scoring is unchanged.

466	4. **Submit.** It enters the bid in the tender portal's configurator and signs it with a TAN from the webmail.

517	## Unlimited Inference
518	
519	We host Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare's Clef for this hackathon, free and with no usage cap. On your laptop, `atira models proxy` gives you a URL and key (setup on [your team page](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/team#team-models)). In test and scored runs it's set up for you. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair.
520	
521	### Qwen3.8-Flash-Next
522	
523	#6 on the [Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index](https://artificialanalysis.ai/models/qwen3-8-flash-next) (open-weight, large models). Multimodal general-purpose LLM. Strong at reasoning, tool calls and reading pages and screenshots, with a 256k context, so it can plan, browse and write the answer.
524	
525	- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 32 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
526	- **Simulated pricing:**
527	  - Input: $0.15 / M tokens
528	  - Cached input: $0.016 / M tokens
529	  - Cache writes: Free
530	  - Output: $0.47 / M tokens
531	- **Precision:** [NVFP4](https://huggingface.co/nvidia/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4) (NVIDIA's checkpoint)
532	
533	Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.
534	
535	```python
536	import os
537	from openai import OpenAI
538	
539	qwen = OpenAI(
540	    base_url=os.environ["QWEN_BASE_URL"],
541	    api_key=os.environ["QWEN_API_KEY"],
542	)
543	reply = qwen.chat.completions.create(
544	    model="qwen",
545	    messages=[{
546	        "role": "user",
547	        "content": "Which button submits?",
548	    }],
549	)
550	```

552	### Cloudflare Clef
553	
554	A multimodal decision model. Give it a state and up to 4 screenshots, then ask it questions: `choice` picks one of your options, `noul` gives the probability of yes, from 0 to 1, and `score` rates on a scale you set. See [Cloudflare's announcement](https://blog.cloudflare.com/clef-decision-models/) and [the benchmarks](https://clef-evals.workers-ai-mle.workers.dev). Worth a try for quick, low-stakes decisions, such as which link to open or whether a page is the right document, while the bigger model reads and reasons.
555	
556	- **Limits:** No usage cap. Up to 16 calls per team at once, across all its runs; more wait in line.
557	- **Simulated pricing:**
558	  - Input: $0.24 / M tokens
559	  - Output: Not priced
560	
561	Scales to zero when idle, but warm-up isn't counted toward a submission's time.
562	
563	```sh
564	curl "$CLEF_BASE_URL/v1/decide" \
565	  -H "Authorization: Bearer $CLEF_API_KEY" \
566	  -H 'content-type: application/json' -d '{
567	  "state": {"page": "Checkout returns 502"},
568	  "questions": {"next": {
569	    "type": "choice",
570	    "instructions": "What next?",

572	      "retry": "Retry the request",
573	      "report": "Report the error"}}}}'

On your machine, `atira models proxy` serves the same APIs on 127.0.0.1, so the same code works in both. Calls from your machine are free, recorded and never ranked. An idle model can take several minutes to wake on its first call, so use long timeouts.

591	## Submitting
592	
593	A submission is your agent as a gzipped tarball. It is reviewed automatically, then run once in the sandbox on the public dataset, and that score ranks your team. Submit as often as you like, one at a time; your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard, and your latest one that passed review goes into the final run.
594	
595	### agent.json
596	
597	```json
598	{
599	  "setup": ["uv", "sync"],
600	  "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"],
601	  "models": ["qwen"]
602	}
603	```
604	
605	Put `agent.json` at the root of the tarball, next to your code and its dependency file. Up to 20 MB compressed. `setup` installs dependencies with network access, within 5 minutes that don't count toward your time; `run` is timed and reaches only the platform and the websites. `"browsers": 1–4` (default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts, each on its own screen. `"models"` lists the hosted models your agent calls; the run waits only for those to warm up (for all of them when it's absent). Node 24 with pnpm and bun, Python 3.12 with uv, and Rust with cargo are installed. The [starter kit](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal skeleton to start from.

643	## Scoring and ranking
644	
645	Every submission is measured on its run in the sandbox.
646	
647	- **Quality:** 0 to 100. Every field of the bid is compared with the one correct answer: tender reference, positions, materials, quantities, unit prices, lead times, discount and total, each position's base price and surcharge per piece, packaging, allocated project bonus, and whether the total adds up.
648	- **Eligibility:** The right tender reference; a wrong decision loses quality points but other correct fields keep their credit. A bid that is not eligible ranks after every eligible one.
649	- **Cost:** Every model call goes through the proxy and is priced per model. There is no budget: at equal quality, cost × time decides.
650	- **Time:** Wall-clock time from the start of the run until the answer is accepted. It weighs as much as cost: halving either halves cost × time.
651	
652	Order: Eligible first → Quality ↓ → Cost × time ↑.
653	
654	Eligible answers rank first, then higher quality. At equal quality, the lower product of cost and time wins, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time as at least 1 s, so among free runs the faster one wins.

662	## Fair play
663	
664	Your agent has to find the answer itself.
665	
666	- Your system must work the answer out from the websites at run time, with a model doing the navigating and deciding. A coding agent reviews every package; hardcoded answers, fixed scripts and crawlers are rejected.
667	- Bring your own model key for Anthropic, OpenAI, OpenRouter, Google, Groq, Mistral, DeepSeek, xAI, Together, Fireworks, kept as a team secret. Every call goes through the run's proxy and is metered at the published prices. Qwen3.8-Flash-Next and Cloudflare Clef are ours, unlimited. Free for you. Each call still adds its simulated price to your run's cost, so the cost ranking stays fair. The sandbox reaches the platform and the websites, nothing else.
668	- At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up to 4 in agent.json ("browsers"), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The sandbox stops any other browser your agent starts.
669	- One submission in flight per team. Submit again once it has finished.

1451	# Answers and scoring
1452	
1453	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
1454	
1455	Each challenge defines its answer format and how quality is scored; the platform measures cost and time and
1456	ranks everyone the same way. Test runs, scored submissions and the scouting logins use the public dataset (the
1457	websites as you see them, with scenario `public-1`), and the leaderboard ranks those results. The correct answer
1458	isn't published; your system has to work it out from the websites. When the hackathon ends, a [final run](#final-run)
1459	on a private dataset weighs most when we pick the [winners](#winners).
1460	
1461	## Per run
1462	
1463	- **Quality** (0 to 100): how right the answer is, by the challenge's scorer.
1464	- **Eligible:** whether the answer meets the challenge's mandatory criteria. For RFQ: the right tender reference;
1465	  a wrong decision (bid or no_bid) costs quality points instead.
1466	- **Cost:** the run's LLM usage, priced per model, in USD.
1467	- **Time:** from the start of your run command to your accepted answer.
1468	
1469	A malformed answer is rejected with a `400` and does not end the run. A well-formed answer is final, even if it
1470	is wrong. A run without an answer scores quality 0 and is not eligible.
1471	
1472	## Leaderboard
1473	
1474	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset and is scored; one run per submission
1475	keeps your model bill down. A submission appears once its run has finished and review is passed; reviewer flags await organizer approval. Each team is ranked by its best
1476	complete submission. The API reports them in its `median_*` fields; with one run per submission, that is
1477	the run's own value.
1478	
1479	1. Eligible before ineligible.
1480	2. Higher quality.
1481	3. Lower cost × time: the submission's cost in USD times its time, with cost counted as at least $0.01 and time
1482	   as at least 1 second. Cost and time weigh the same: halving your model bill counts as much as halving your run
1483	   time, and among free runs the faster one wins.
1484	4. The submission ID, when everything above is equal.
1485	
1486	On the leaderboard's plot, each team is a dot, quality against cost or time; the dotted line is the Pareto front,
1487	the teams no other eligible team beats on both.
1488	
1489	Test runs on the public scenario `public-1` show the points for each part of the answer, never the expected
1490	values. Scored runs show quality, eligibility, cost and time without a breakdown.
1491	
1492	## Final run
1493	
1494	When the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it, and each run's brief states the bid rules. It ranks in the same order as above. Build an agent that works the
1495	answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
1496	
1497	## Winners
1498	
1499	We pick the winners on three things, roughly in this order:
1500	
1501	1. Performance on the private dataset (the final run).
1502	2. Performance on the public dataset (the leaderboard).
1503	3. The elegance of the system.
1504	
1505	It is the latest submission, not the best one: your best submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
1506	latest one that passed review goes into the final run. The final run's results stay with the organizers until they
1507	publish them. Then the leaderboard shows the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", with each team's
1508	public-dataset result and its change in rank beside them, and the public-dataset board stays at `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public` (Markdown:
1509	`leaderboard.md?dataset=public`; API: `GET /v1/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`).
1510	
1511	## RFQ scoring
1512	
1513	The brief states the calculation rules. Each position has four optional fields that earn independent points:
1514	`base_unit_price` (the EUR scale price per piece before discount), `surcharge_per_unit` (material surcharge plus
1515	ordinary and allocated setup cost per piece, before discount), `packaging_per_unit`, and `rebate_total` (the
1516	project-bonus credit for the **entire position**). Leave a field blank if unanswered; enter zero for a known zero.
1517	The same calculation rules and answer format apply to the public and private datasets. You can also explicitly
1518	omit unfinished positions in the form; completed fields retain their credit. You must sign and submit to score.
1519	
1520	| Part (a bid) | Points |
1521	| --- | --- |
1522	| Decision | 5 |
1523	| Tender reference | 5 |
1524	| Discount percent | 5 |
1525	| Total net (to the cent, consistent with the positions) | 5 |
1526	| Arithmetic (every position, and a total that is their sum) | 5 |
1527	| Withdrawn Q&A quantity check (when present) | 5 |
1528	| Dated metal-index check (when present) | 5 |
1529	| Positions (split evenly): material 20 %, quantity 15 %, base price 15 %, surcharge 10 %, packaging 10 %, project bonus 10 %, unit price 10 %, lead time 10 % | 75 minus the checks above |
1530	
1531	
1532	For a no_bid case: decision 75, tender reference 5, no positions 5, a total of 0 15. A wrong decision costs its
1533	points but leaves the other fields their credit.
1534	
1535	Money is compared to the cent. Positions are matched by their position number; extra or duplicate positions cost
1536	one position's share each.
1537	
1538	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
1539	
1540	The final runs your latest passed submission on the private set. The default is one attempt.
1541	Before the final run starts, opt in to **Best of 3** on your team page or run
1542	`atira final --best-of 3` (`--best-of 1` opts out). `atira status` shows the choice.
1543	When the final run starts, each team's choice is fixed, including teams still in review.
1544	Opted-in teams get up to three attempts on the same private scenario(s). Your **single best complete attempt**
1545	counts: eligible first, then higher quality, then lower cost × time, with the leaderboard's usual floors.
1546	It is not an average, and a failed attempt does not outweigh a better successful one.
1547	Every attempt is kept. Your team sees its own attempts' logs (private values masked) and, once the organizers publish the final, the results.
1548	Calls using your own model keys can cost up to **3×**. The public leaderboard remains one run per submission
1549	on the public scenario. Review, flags and disqualification work as for any submission.
1550	
1551	Flagged results are hidden from the public leaderboard by default. **Show flagged** on the page (or `?flagged=1` on
1552	the leaderboard API) lists them beside the approved ones, tagged "flagged: waiting for an organizer" and without a
1553	rank, so showing them does not change other ranks. An organizer pass makes a flagged result count normally.

1559	# How a run works
1560	
1561	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
1562	
1563	A run is one attempt at one scenario of one challenge. It starts with a run token, gives your agent a task and
1564	logins for the challenge's websites, and ends when your agent submits its answer or time runs out. Test runs and
1565	scored runs both run your package in the [sandbox](#scored-run); you develop on your own machine with the scouting
1566	logins.
1567	
1568	## Develop locally, then test in the sandbox
1569	
1570	RFQ has one public scenario, `public-1`: the websites as you see them.
1571	
1572	1. **Develop locally** against the public websites with the scouting logins the organizers publish:
1573	   `eval "$(atira scout --env)"` (in PowerShell: `atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression`) sets
1574	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` (the websites and their logins, the JSON a run gets), each website's URL as
1575	   `CHALLENGE_SITE_<ID>_URL`, and `CHALLENGE_SCOUTING`, the `brief`, `access`, `submission` and `answer_schema` of
1576	   `GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/scouting` as JSON (`CHALLENGE_SCOUTING_URL` is that address). There is no run token.
1577	   Where the platform hosts models, they need no key: `--env` also exports each one's base URL and key, pointed at
1578	   `atira models proxy` on your computer with `local` as the key, so run `atira login` once, then keep
1579	   `atira models proxy` running in another terminal. Those calls are free, recorded and never ranked. Any other
1580	   provider takes your own key.
1581	   Nothing done with these logins counts.
1582	   A bid entered on the tender portal is acknowledged without counting.
1583	2. **Test in the sandbox:** `atira test-run ./my-agent` uploads your package, starts a test run on `public-1` and
1584	   opens its run page live. It runs in the same sandbox as a scored run, but for up to 2 hours instead of 20 minutes (keep it under
1585	   20 to be safe), and the run page shows its
1586	   score with the full breakdown. `atira cancel` stops it early.
1587	
1588	## Inside a run
1589	
1590	1. **Read the task:** `GET $CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` with the header `x-api-key: $CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN`
1591	   returns:
1592	   - `brief`: the task statement in markdown, with the rules;
1593	   - `access`: one entry per website: `siteId`, `url`, and `credentials` (`username`, `password`);
1594	   - `submission`: where the answer goes: `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` (POST it to that URL) or
1595	     `{"kind": "site", "siteId": ..., "url": ...}` (submit it on that website, e.g. RFQ's configurator);
1596	   - `answer_url` (API submissions only) and `answer_schema` (JSON Schema of the answer);
1597	   - `started_at`, `expires_at`, and what the run has spent on LLM calls so far.
1598	   - `llm_proxy_url`: the model proxy base with this run's token, `llm_providers` and `llm_base_urls` (each
1599	     provider's proxy base), and `llm_env` (the SDK base-URL variables the run step gets).
1600	   Keep the token secret: it is your agent's identity for this run.
1601	2. **Work:** your agent logs into the websites with those credentials and collects what it needs. Its LLM calls
1602	   go through our metering proxy: a hosted model's with the run token its key variable already holds, any other
1603	   provider's with your own key (below).
1604	3. **Answer** through the run's `submission` target. For an `api` target, `POST` the answer as JSON to
1605	   `answer_url` with the same `x-api-key` header. For a `site` target, submit it on that website: the site
1606	   forwards it to the platform, shows the same validation issues in German, and confirms with a receipt.
1607	   - `400` with `issues`: the answer is malformed. Nothing is recorded, the clock keeps running, fix it and send
1608	     it again.
1609	   - `202`: accepted and final. The run ends, the token and the website logins stop working, and a test run
1610	     returns its score and breakdown. Your agent then has 10 seconds to exit before the platform stops it.
1611	
1612	Site logins are issued per run and only work while that run is live. Send tokens in the `x-api-key` header
1613	(`Authorization: Bearer` works too). Send a User-Agent of your own: the edge in
1614	front of the API currently refuses Python's default `Python-urllib/…` agent with 403. Test runs last up to 2 hours.
1615	
1616	## LLM calls
1617	
1618	Use the [hosted models](#how-cost-is-measured), which are free, or bring your own key for any provider and model.
1619	Every call goes through our proxy, which forwards it unchanged and only measures it: a provider you bring bills your
1620	own key, and the ranking uses what the call costs at the published prices. A scored run's sandbox reaches only our
1621	API and the challenge's websites, so its model calls work only through the proxy; test runs are metered the same way.
1622	
1623	The run token sits in the proxy path, so your key keeps its usual header and an SDK needs only a base URL:
1624	
1625	```
1626	$API/llm/run/<run token>/<provider>/<the provider's own API path>
1627	```
1628	
1629	`llm_proxy_url` is the run's proxy, `<run API>/llm/run/<run token>`; in a test or scored run it is `$LLM_PROXY_URL`. Built-in providers:
1630	
1631	| Provider | Forwards to | Base URL for its SDK or an OpenAI-compatible client |
1632	| --- | --- | --- |
1633	| `anthropic` | `https://api.anthropic.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
1634	| `openai` | `https://api.openai.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
1635	| `openrouter` | `https://openrouter.ai/api` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openrouter/v1` |
1636	| `google` | `https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google` (Gemini SDK), `…/google/v1beta/openai` |
1637	| `groq` | `https://api.groq.com/openai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/groq/v1` (use an OpenAI client) |
1638	| `mistral` | `https://api.mistral.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral/v1` |
1639	| `deepseek` | `https://api.deepseek.com` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/deepseek/v1` |
1640	| `xai` | `https://api.x.ai` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/xai/v1` (HTTP API; the gRPC `xai-sdk` cannot use the proxy) |
1641	| `together` | `https://api.together.xyz` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
1642	| `fireworks` | `https://api.fireworks.ai/inference` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/fireworks/v1` |
1643	
1644	The organizers may add providers; `llm_providers` lists them all, the models the platform hosts itself included,
1645	each under its own id with its base URL in `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`. Any path under a provider's base works
1646	(messages, chat completions, responses, embeddings, model listings) with the request's method and body intact.
1647	
1648	### Your key
1649	
1650	Send your provider key the way the provider expects it: `x-api-key` (Anthropic), `Authorization: Bearer`
1651	(OpenAI and compatible providers), `x-goog-api-key` or `?key=` (Gemini), or `api-key`. The proxy forwards it
1652	unchanged and never stores, logs or returns it. For test and scored runs, keep it as a [team secret](#team-secrets),
1653	not in your package: we store packages and the review agent reads them.
1654	
1655	With the base-URL variables set, the providers' SDKs need no changes: OpenAI's reads `OPENAI_BASE_URL` and sends
1656	`OPENAI_API_KEY` as `Authorization: Bearer`, Anthropic's reads `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` and sends `ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`
1657	as `x-api-key`:
1658	
1659	```python
1660	from openai import OpenAI
1661	
1662	client = OpenAI()  # reads OPENAI_BASE_URL and OPENAI_API_KEY
1663	```
1664	
1665	A client that cannot set the provider's own header may send the key as `x-provider-key`; the proxy forwards it in
1666	the provider's header. For Google's Gemini SDK, set the HTTP base URL explicitly:
1667	
1668	```python
1669	import os
1670	from google import genai
1671	
1672	client = genai.Client(api_key=os.environ["GEMINI_API_KEY"],
1673	    http_options={"base_url": os.environ["LLM_PROXY_URL"] + "/google"})
1674	```
1675	
1676	```javascript
1677	import { GoogleGenAI } from "@google/genai"
1678	
1679	const client = new GoogleGenAI({ apiKey: process.env.GEMINI_API_KEY,
1680	  httpOptions: { baseUrl: process.env.LLM_PROXY_URL + "/google" } })
1681	```
1682	
1683	A request without a key of its own gets `401` "Add your <provider> API key to the request.", unless the
1684	organizers pay for that provider: then the proxy adds their key to a run's calls. In that case a scored run's
1685	key variable for that provider (for example `OPENAI_API_KEY`) holds the run token as a placeholder, so SDKs
1686	start, unless you have a team secret by that name; the proxy never forwards the token.
1687	
1688	**Development outside runs:** with your personal token you may use the proxy without a run, at
1689	`$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the header `x-atira-team-key: <token>`, or at `$API/llm/team/<token>/<provider>/…`
1690	(prefer the header: a token lasts 90 days, and URLs end up in logs). Bring your own key; this usage is recorded
1691	for your team and never ranked. Older clients may still call `$API/llm/<provider>/…` with the run token in
1692	`x-api-key` and the provider key in `x-provider-key`. Without a run token or personal token, the proxy answers
1693	`401`.
1694	
1695	A request body may be up to 32 MiB (`413` above that), enough for several full-screen screenshots and a long
1696	context.
1697	
1698	### How cost is measured
1699	
1700	Every call is recorded. Reported usage, including cached input and thinking tokens, is priced at each
1701	provider's published per-token prices for that model, with any deployment-specific prices published by the organizers.
1702	An upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. OpenRouter reports one for every call (send
1703	`"usage": {"include": true}` with older clients), so models without a published price are accepted there; a call
1704	that reports no cost is charged at the highest published price. Elsewhere, unpriced models and models outside
1705	a configured allowlist are refused before forwarding. Streamed calls count too: the proxy asks OpenAI-compatible
1706	providers for a stream's usage (`stream_options.include_usage`), so a streamed chat completion ends with one more
1707	chunk with empty `choices` and the usage. A stream cut off before its usage, or one whose provider reports none, counts
1708	an estimate from the text that arrived and from the request, about four characters per token; a client that hangs up
1709	early is still billed for everything the provider sends. There is no spending limit. Model listings and other
1710	endpoints without inference usage cost nothing; Anthropic `count_tokens` also costs nothing. All network and
1711	fair-play rules still apply, including when using provider-side tools.
1712	
1713	The models the platform hosts itself (`GET /v1/models/status` lists them with their prices) are free to use, never
1714	charged; each call counts toward your run's cost at simulated API prices, so the cost ranking stays honest.
1715	
1716	### Team secrets
1717	
1718	Team secrets are environment variables for your agent's run step in test runs and scored runs, such as
1719	`OPENAI_API_KEY`. Manage them on the team page under Secrets, or with your personal token:
1720	
1721	```sh
1722	curl -X PUT -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/json" \
1723	  --data '{"value": "sk-…"}' "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
1724	curl -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets"   # names and dates only
1725	curl -X DELETE -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" "$API/v1/teams/me/secrets/OPENAI_API_KEY"
1726	```
1727	
1728	Values are encrypted, never shown again and redacted from run logs; saving a name again replaces its value.
1729	Setup never receives them. Names are uppercase letters, digits and underscores, starting with a letter, and
1730	cannot be platform variables (`CHALLENGE_*`, `*_BASE_URL`, `*_SERVER_URL`, `*_PROXY`, `LLM_PROXY_URL`,
1731	`CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS`, `BROWSER_COUNT`, `PATH`, `HOME`, `DISPLAY`, …). A team keeps at most 20; each value is 16 characters to 4 KB long.
1732	
1733	## Scored run
1734	
1735	Each scored submission runs once in the sandbox on the public dataset (RFQ's `public-1`) and is scored; that run
1736	ranks on the leaderboard. The final run at the end of the hackathon uses the same sandbox on a private dataset (see
1737	[Submitting](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md#what-happens-next)). Runs are created from your uploaded package. The sandbox is
1738	a Linux VM with a desktop at 1280×800, a **headful Chromium** already open with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on
1739	`127.0.0.1:9222` (or up to four, see [Browsers](#browsers)) and these toolchains, ready for your user:
1740	
1741	- **TypeScript and JavaScript:** Node 24 (runs `.ts` files directly), npm, pnpm and bun.
1742	- **Python:** Python 3.12 and uv (`uv venv`, `uv pip install`, `uv run`); there is no system pip.
1743	- **Rust:** stable Rust (1.99) with cargo. Fetch crates during setup; the run is offline except for the platform
1744	  and the websites.
1745	- gcc, make, git, curl and jq.
1746	
1747	1. **Setup (not counted toward your time, up to 5 minutes):** your `setup` command runs with network access but without any credentials, e.g. to install dependencies.
1748	2. **Model warm-up (not counted toward your time):** the models the platform hosts itself, when it offers any, scale
1749	   to zero when nobody uses them, and waking one takes one to eight minutes. The platform wakes them as soon as your
1750	   run leaves the queue and starts your run only once they're warm (at most 10 minutes after setup), so a cold start
1751	   never counts toward your time. The run's log says when they're warm. While runs are active, the platform keeps
1752	   them warm. `"models"` in `agent.json` lists the ones your agent system calls, by their `provider` id from
1753	   `GET /v1/models/status` (the start page shows it too); the run waits for those alone, and `"models": []` starts it
1754	   right after setup:
1755	
1756	   ```json
1757	   {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": []}
1758	   ```
1759	
1760	   Without it the run waits for every hosted model. Anything else, such as an unknown id, rejects the package with
1761	   `Invalid agent.json: models: …` and the ids it takes. It decides only the wait: your run may call any hosted model
1762	   whatever it lists, but one it didn't list may still be waking.
1763	
1764	   **If a hosted model fails mid-run:** retry failed calls, as with any provider; a short outage is yours to ride out.
1765	   If our models were down for most of the run (from the first failed call on, a 5xx from our model or a lost
1766	   connection to it, at least 8 in 10 of the run's hosted-model calls failed, over at least half its time) and the run
1767	   then ended without an answer, the platform failed, not your agent system: the run doesn't count toward ranking or
1768	   any limit, and a scored run starts again once by itself. A
1769	   run that answered keeps its result.
1770	3. **Run (timed):** your `run` command starts with this environment. The clock starts here.
1771	
1772	| Variable | Value |
1773	| --- | --- |
1774	| `CHALLENGE_API_URL` | the API; read your task at `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/v1/runs/current` |
1775	| `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | the run token |
1776	| `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS` | the websites with this run's logins, as JSON: the same as `access` |
1777	| `LLM_PROXY_URL` | `$CHALLENGE_API_URL/llm/run/$CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` |
1778	| `<MODEL>_BASE_URL`, `<MODEL>_API_KEY` | for each model the platform hosts (`GET /v1/models/status`; the start page names them): its base URL through the proxy, under `$LLM_PROXY_URL/<provider>`, and the run token as its key |
1779	| `ANTHROPIC_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/anthropic` |
1780	| `OPENAI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/openai/v1` |
1781	| `GOOGLE_GEMINI_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/google`; set the Gemini SDK's HTTP base URL explicitly as above |
1782	| `MISTRAL_SERVER_URL`, `TOGETHER_BASE_URL` | `$LLM_PROXY_URL/mistral`, `$LLM_PROXY_URL/together/v1` |
1783	| your [team secrets](#team-secrets) | for example `OPENAI_API_KEY` with your own key |
1784	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222`, browser 1 |
1785	| `CDP_URLS` | every browser's CDP URL in order, as a JSON array: `["http://127.0.0.1:9222"]` for one browser |
1786	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | how many browsers the sandbox started: `1` unless `agent.json` asks for more |
1787	| `DISPLAY` | `:1`, browser 1's screen; browser n is on `:n` |
1788	| `HTTP_PROXY`, `HTTPS_PROXY` (and lowercase) | `http://127.0.0.1:3128`, the only way out of the sandbox |
1789	| `NO_PROXY` | `localhost,127.0.0.1` (CDP stays local) |
1790	
1791	The platform sets no API key variables of its own, except the run-token placeholder for a provider the
1792	organizers pay for (above). `setup` runs first, with network (install your dependencies there) but without the
1793	run's variables or your team secrets, and nothing it starts survives into the run. The run itself reaches only our API and the challenge's websites,
1794	through that proxy; Chromium is already configured to use it. A scored run of RFQ has 20 minutes; a run that
1795	ends without an answer scores 0.

1797	## Browsers
1798	
1799	The sandbox starts one browser unless `agent.json` asks for more, up to four:
1800	
1801	```json
1802	{"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "browsers": 3}
1803	```
1804	
1805	`browsers` is a whole number from 1 to 4; anything else rejects the package with
1806	`Invalid agent.json: browsers: must be a whole number from 1 to 4`. Browser n is its own headful Chromium with its
1807	own profile, on display `:n` (1280×800) with the Chrome DevTools Protocol on port 9221 + n (9222 to 9225), behind
1808	the same proxy as browser 1. All of them are ready before the clock starts. `CDP_URL` stays browser 1, `CDP_URLS` lists all of
1809	them in order, and `BROWSER_COUNT` says how many there are. With three:
1810	
1811	| Variable | Value |
1812	| --- | --- |
1813	| `CDP_URL` | `http://127.0.0.1:9222` |
1814	| `CDP_URLS` | `["http://127.0.0.1:9222","http://127.0.0.1:9223","http://127.0.0.1:9224"]` |
1815	| `BROWSER_COUNT` | `3` |
1816	
1817	**At most 4 browsers run at a time:** ask for up to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts
1818	inside them freely, and don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included. The scored sandbox enforces it:
1819	any other browser the agent starts is stopped within seconds, and the run's logs say so with
1820	`[platform] stopped a browser the agent started: at most 4 run at a time; use the browsers from CDP_URLS`. Every
1821	browser then is one the platform can show and record: test runs show them side by side while they run, with a
1822	recording of each afterwards.
1823	
1824	On your own machine, developing with the scouting logins, `CDP_URLS` is not set and your agent starts its own
1825	browsers.

1831	# Building your agent
1832	
1833	Your agent system has to be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the information and makes
1834	the decisions, at run time. How is up to you: drive the browser through the DOM, through pixels, or both; use one
1835	model or several, in parallel if you like; give the model tools and helpers for the browser, parsing, arithmetic and
1836	checks. The model chooses where to go, what to search for and which documents matter. Rejected in review: a fixed
1837	script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback, and a crawler that collects the
1838	websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
1839	
1840	## The browser
1841	
1842	In the sandbox a headful Chromium runs on the desktop (`DISPLAY=:1`, 1280×800) with CDP on
1843	`127.0.0.1:9222`.
1844	
1845	- **DOM agents:** attach with Playwright (`chromium.connect_over_cdp(CDP_URL)`) or any CDP client.
1846	- **Pixel agents:** take screenshots and send mouse and keyboard input to the desktop (`xdotool` and
1847	  ImageMagick's `import` are installed), for example to drive Claude's computer-use tool.
1848	- **Locally:** without `CDP_URL`, launch your own Chromium. The websites are the same: `eval "$(atira scout --env)"`
1849	  gives your agent the scouting logins in `CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS`, the way a run gets its logins.
1850	
1851	### Several browsers
1852	
1853	To work on several websites at once, ask for up to four browsers in `agent.json`:
1854	
1855	```json
1856	{"setup": ["npm", "ci"], "run": ["node", "agent.js"], "browsers": 2}
1857	```
1858	
1859	Each is its own Chromium on its own screen (browser n on `DISPLAY=:n`), and `CDP_URLS` lists their CDP URLs in
1860	order (`CDP_URL` stays the first). With Playwright:
1861	
1862	```javascript
1863	import { chromium } from "playwright"
1864	
1865	const sites = JSON.parse(process.env.CHALLENGE_SITE_ACCESS)
1866	const browsers = await Promise.all(JSON.parse(process.env.CDP_URLS).map((url) => chromium.connectOverCDP(url)))
1867	const pages = browsers.map((browser) => browser.contexts()[0].pages()[0])
1868	await Promise.all([pages[0].goto(sites[0].url), pages[1].goto(sites[1].url)])
1869	```
1870	
1871	At most 4 browsers run at a time. Use tabs (`context.newPage()`) and browser contexts (`browser.newContext()`)
1872	inside them as freely as you like, but don't start browsers of your own, headless ones included: the sandbox stops
1873	them and says so in the run's logs. A test run shows its browsers side by side while it runs and keeps a recording
1874	of each. Locally there is no `CDP_URLS`: on your machine your agent starts its own browsers.
1875	
1876	## Models
1877	
1878	The hosted models are free to use. Every run gets `QWEN_BASE_URL` and `QWEN_API_KEY` for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next, an
1879	OpenAI-compatible chat model with tool calls and images; on your machine `atira scout --env` sets the same variables,
1880	pointed at `atira models proxy`. You can also bring your own key for any provider through the metering proxy;
1881	[how cost is measured](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#how-cost-is-measured) has the details. After quality you are ranked on cost × time, so a cheaper model or a faster run that gets the answer right moves you
1882	up.
1883	
1884	## What makes it hard, on purpose
1885	
1886	The websites are designed to trip agents up: cookie walls, flaky error pages that need a retry, expiring sessions
1887	that send you back to the login, documents inside iframes and ZIP files, popups that close themselves, paging and
1888	"load more" buttons, look-alike records, superseded versions shown first, a timezone that is not yours. Treat
1889	every page as adversarial and verify what you read.
1890	
1891	## Tips
1892	
1893	- Read the brief's rules carefully: they define the one correct answer.
1894	- Keep what the model reads small: page text without duplicated labels, only the parts you need.
1895	- Use prompt caching for your system prompt and tool definitions.
1896	- Re-read a page after every action that changes it; pages update asynchronously.
1897	- Drive four browsers in parallel, one per website (`"browsers": 4`, see [Several browsers](#several-browsers)):
1898	  reading the four sites at once speeds up each run and your iteration, at the cost of more complex code.
1899	- Validate your answer against `answer_schema` before sending it; a `400` costs only time.
1900	- Submit before the clock runs out: a scored run has 20 minutes (`expires_at` in the run). Every part of the answer
1901	  scores on its own, so have your agent submit its best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
1902	  searching; a run that ends without an answer scores 0.
1903	- Develop against the public websites locally (`atira scout --env`), then test in the sandbox (`atira test-run`):
1904	  a test run shows the full score breakdown, so use it to find what your agent gets wrong.
1905	- Work the answer out from the websites: the final run, which weighs most for the winners, uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it.
1906	
1907	## Starter kit
1908	
1909	[`starter-kit/`](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/starter-kit.tar.gz) is a minimal Python skeleton, not an agent: it reads the run and
1910	submits an answer, attaches to the run's browsers over CDP with Playwright, and shows one call to each hosted model.
1911	Your agent goes in `solve()` in `agent.py`; out of the box it exits without an answer. Start from it or from scratch.
1912	
1913	---
1914	
1915	Source: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/fair-play.md
1916	
1917	# Fair play
1918	
1919	**Rules at a glance**
1920	
1921	You submit an agentic system: one agent or several. In the sandbox it does the whole job on its own: finds what it needs on the four websites, works out the bid and submits it. Nobody helps it during a run.
1922	
1923	**Not allowed**
1924	
1925	- **Hardcoding:** copying values from the websites into your package (prices, material numbers, totals, discounts, logins, TANs), including in prompts and notes, also as defaults or fallbacks. Using what the task brief tells every team, like the sales director's mailbox, is fine.
1926	- **Pre-solving:** working out the answer yourself, or having an AI assistant do it, and putting the result in your package. Exploring the sites with an assistant is fine.
1927	- **Scripts instead of agents:** a fixed click path, or a crawler that grabs everything for one model call. A model has to choose where to go, what to search for and what matters.
1928	- **Outside help during a run:** contacting anything besides our platform and the four websites, calling a model other than through our proxy (your own API keys work through it), running a model inside the sandbox, or starting your own browsers (use the up to 4 provided). Setup may install dependencies.
1929	
1930	**How it's checked:** an AI reviewer reads every submitted package before its scored run. Unclear cases are flagged and stay off the leaderboard until an organizer has looked. The final runs on websites and data your system hasn't seen.
1931	
1932	The details follow.
1933	
1934	## Allowed
1935	
1936	- Any agent design; the free hosted models, or any provider and model with your own key, through the proxy; any
1937	  amount of tokens.
1938	  The proxy forwards your calls unchanged and measures them: reported usage is metered at the published model
1939	  prices, and an upstream-reported USD cost takes precedence. See [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls)
1940	  for SDK configuration.
1941	- Keeping your model key as a [team secret](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#team-secrets) rather than in your package.
1942	- Your own code, prompts and tools; open-source libraries installed during setup.
1943	- Using what you learned with the scouting logins and in test runs about how the websites work.
1944	- Up to 4 browsers at a time: ask for them with `"browsers"` in `agent.json` and use as many tabs and browser
1945	  contexts inside them as you like.
1946	
1947	## Not allowed
1948	
1949	- Hardcoding values copied from the public scenario or its websites into code, config, prompts or notes, including defaults and fallbacks: tender references, material numbers, prices, totals, discounts, logins and TANs. Facts the task brief states for every scenario, such as the sales director's mailbox, are
1950	  rules you may use.
1951	- A scripted solution. Your agent system must be agentic: a model decides where to go on the websites, finds the
1952	  information and makes the decisions. Code can help it (browser control, parsing, arithmetic, checks, reading a
1953	  page or document the model chose, paging through results it asked for), and several agents and browsers may work
1954	  in parallel. Rejected: a fixed script that clicks through known pages with the model unused or only as a fallback,
1955	  and a crawler that collects the websites and hands everything to the model at the end.
1956	- Bundling or running a local model, or reaching any model other than through the proxy.
1957	- Contacting hosts other than the API and the challenge's websites, or trying to get data out of the sandbox.
1958	- Starting browsers of your own in the sandbox, headless ones included. At most 4 browsers run at a time: ask for up
1959	  to 4 in `agent.json` (`"browsers"`), use tabs and browser contexts inside them freely, and don't start others.
1960	  On your own machine (developing with the scouting logins) your agent starts its own browsers; that is up to you.
1961	- Attacking the platform, the websites, the sandbox or other teams; sharing scored-run data.
1962	
1963	## How it is checked
1964	
1965	- **Package review before any scored run:** an AI code reviewer, a coding agent that reads your whole package in an
1966	  isolated VM. Outcomes: passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged package still runs and scores, but its
1967	  result stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it
1968	  marked "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Notes and docs addressed to the reviewer are not evidence of compliance
1969	  and do not count against you on their own. Instructions trying to steer the reviewer's verdict do.
1970	  The reviewer's reasons stay with the organizers: your team reads "Flagged by the reviewing agent" or "Rejected by
1971	  the reviewing agent". Someone from Atira looks at flagged packages shortly and unflags a misdetection; if you think
1972	  a reject is one, contact the Atira team.
1973	- **The organizers decide flagged packages, and can look at any submission:** they pass it, add an internal note
1974	  (this changes nothing you or the leaderboard see) or disqualify it. A disqualified submission and its runs read
1975	  "disqualified": it leaves the leaderboard and the final run, its runs still going stop, and your team page shows the
1976	  organizers' reason.
1977	- **Hardcoded values:** the reviewer rejects copied scenario values in code or config, even in defaults or fallbacks.
1978	- **The final run** uses a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a
1979	  supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software,
1980	  with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently
1981	  across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. That run weighs most when we pick the
1982	  winners, so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to the public scenario.
1983	- **The sandbox** reaches only our API and the websites, so every model call passes the proxy and is measured.
1984	  Your team secrets reach only the timed run step and are redacted from its logs.
1985	- **Website logins** exist only for a live run and stop working when it ends.
1986	- **Browsers:** the sandbox stops any browser your agent starts beyond the ones it asked for and notes it in the
1987	  run's logs: `[platform] stopped a browser the agent started`.
1988	- **Everything measured** (tokens, cost, time, the answer) is recorded by the platform, never reported by you.
1989	
1990	Breaking these rules gets the submission rejected before it runs, or removed later; repeated or deliberate attempts
1991	get the team disqualified.
1992	
1993	## Flagged results
1994	
1995	A flagged result stays off the public leaderboard until an organizer passes it. **Show flagged** on the leaderboard
1996	lists flagged results, without a rank.
1997	
1998	---
1999	
2000	Source: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/submitting.md
2001	
2002	# Submitting
2003	
2004	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
2005	
2006	You submit your agent system as a gzipped tarball. We review it, run it once in the sandbox on the public dataset
2007	and score it. That run determines its rank on the leaderboard. When the hackathon ends, your latest submission that
2008	passed review runs once more, on a private dataset, in the [final run](#what-happens-next), which weighs most when we pick the winners.
2009	
2010	## Package layout
2011	
2012	```
2013	agent.json          {"setup": ["uv", "sync"], "run": ["uv", "run", "python", "agent.py"], "models": ["qwen"]}
2014	pyproject.toml      (or package.json, requirements.txt, ...)
2015	agent.py            your code
2016	```
2017	
2018	- `agent.json` at the root: `setup` (optional) and `run`, each an argv array. Both run in the package directory.
2019	  `browsers` (optional, 1 to 4, default 1) is how many browsers the sandbox starts for the run; see
2020	  [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#browsers). `models` (optional) lists the hosted models your agent system calls,
2021	  by provider id, all of them by default: the run's clock waits for those to warm up, and `[]` starts it right after
2022	  setup; see [the run contract](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/run-contract.md#scored-run).
2023	- At most 20 MB compressed; regular files only.
2024	- No secrets: the run gets everything it needs from the environment.
2025	
2026	## Upload
2027	
2028	```
2029	tar czf agent.tar.gz -C my-agent .
2030	curl --data-binary @agent.tar.gz \
2031	  -H "x-api-key: $ATIRA_TOKEN" -H "content-type: application/gzip" \
2032	  $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions
2033	```
2034	
2035	The response (`202`) has your submission's id. Review is still pending and no runs exist yet: follow it with
2036	`GET $API/v1/challenges/rfq/submissions` for the review result and run ids, or watch the leaderboard.
2037	
2038	`$ATIRA_TOKEN` is your personal token: `atira login` signs the [CLI](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/cli.md) in through the browser, and
2039	`atira token` prints the token (or sign in with plain curl, as the [API guide](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/api.md#signing-in) shows).
2040	
2041	Or let the CLI pack, check and upload the folder: `atira submit my-agent` (and `atira test-run my-agent` for a
2042	test run). It leaves out `.git`, `node_modules` and what `.gitignore` excludes. In a terminal, `submit` then opens
2043	your team page, which shows the review and links each scored run as it starts, and `test-run` opens the run page.
2044	
2045	## Test it in the sandbox first
2046	
2047	Upload the same tarball as a test run ("Test runs" on your team page, or
2048	`POST $API/v1/challenges/rfq/rehearsals` with the same headers). It runs once in the scored-run sandbox against
2049	the public scenario `public-1`, scored with the points for each part of the answer. Its live view shows the
2050	browser (a frame about every 1.5 s, or the live screen where available), the phases, every model call,
2051	and your logs as the agent prints them. Afterwards the recorded video stays available to
2052	your team. Up to two test runs at a time per team. `atira test-run my-agent` uploads it, starts the run
2053	and opens it live; `atira cancel` (or Cancel run on the run page) stops a run that has not finished, and frees its
2054	test-run slot at once.
2055	
2056	## Linking your GitHub repository
2057	
2058	The organizers ask each team to link the GitHub repository it builds its agent in, so they can review the
2059	code, for example to compare a winning submission with its source. On your team page, the captain chooses
2060	Connect a GitHub repository, installs the organizers' GitHub App on the account that owns the repository
2061	(granting it only that repository is enough), and picks the repository. Every member sees the linked repository,
2062	who linked it and when; the captain can switch or unlink it at any time.
2063	
2064	The app only reads the contents of the repositories you grant it; it cannot push, open issues or change
2065	settings. Linking does not change how you submit: scored submissions and test runs are still the tarballs
2066	described above. To withdraw access completely, unlink the repository and uninstall the app in your GitHub
2067	settings.
2068	
2069	## Watching your submission
2070	
2071	Each scored run has a live view with its phase, timer, model calls, tokens and cost. On the public dataset it also
2072	shows your team the browser (frames, and the live screen where available), the logs and errors
2073	unredacted and the scenario id, and the recording afterwards. The final run on the private dataset shows its
2074	screen, frames and recordings to the organizers only; your team reads its logs and errors with private values
2075	masked as `[private]`.
2076	
2077	## Resubmitting
2078	
2079	Submit as often as you like, one at a time: while a submission is still in review or has unfinished runs, the
2080	next upload is refused with `429`. Your **best complete** submission holds your place on the leaderboard; your
2081	**latest** one that passed review goes into the final run. Your other submissions stay in your history at
2082	`$API/team`. Cancelling a submission's scored run ends that submission: it never completes, the leaderboard ignores it, and you
2083	can submit again.
2084	
2085	## What happens next
2086	
2087	1. **Review:** passed, flagged or rejected (no runs). A flagged submission still runs and scores, but its result
2088	   stays off the public leaderboard and the activity feed until an organizer passes it; your team sees it marked
2089	   "flagged: waiting for an organizer". Your team sees the outcome, not the reviewer's reasons. The organizers can
2090	   still pass or disqualify a submission later; a disqualified one reads "disqualified", leaves the leaderboard and
2091	   the final run, and your team page gives the organizers' reason.
2092	2. **Scored run:** one run in a fresh sandbox on the public dataset, setup first (up to 5 minutes, not counted),
2093	   then your run command (timed).
2094	3. **Ranking:** once the run has finished and review is passed, your submission appears on the leaderboard with its quality, cost and
2095	   time; ineligible answers rank after every eligible one.
2096	4. **Final run:** when the hackathon ends, the organizers run every team's latest submission that passed review
2097	   (organizers resolve outstanding reviewer flags before the final run starts; rejected and disqualified ones don't count) once by default (or best of three if you opt in before the final run starts) on a private dataset that is similar, not the same. It has the same jobs (a tender portal, a supplier portal, an ERP and a webmail inbox), the same bid rules and the same answer format, but different software, with a different look, navigation and site names, other content and data, and the information split differently across them. Your agent has to handle it as it finds it. It is the latest one, not the best one.
2098	   That run weighs most when we pick the winners ([Winners](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#winners)), so build a system that works the answer out from the websites, not one tuned to
2099	   the public scenario. Its results stay with the organizers until they publish them; then the leaderboard shows
2100	   the final results, tagged "Private dataset · final", and the public-dataset board stays at
2101	   `$API/challenges/rfq/leaderboard?dataset=public`.
2102	
2103	## Final private evaluation: one attempt or best of three
2104	
2105	The final runs your latest passed submission once, or up to three times if you opt in to **Best of 3** on your team
2106	page before the final starts (`atira final --best-of 3`). Your best attempt counts. Details:
2107	[Answers and scoring](https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/scoring.md#final-private-evaluation-one-attempt-or-best-of-three).
2108	
2109	---
2110	
2111	Source: https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai/docs/demo-day.md
2112	
2113	# Demo day
2114	
2115	> In this document, `$API` is https://ehl-challenge.atira.ai (the CLI and API guide call it `$ATIRA_API`).
2116	
2117	The best teams run their agent live on stage against the public scenario while the room watches the live run
2118	view.
2119	
2120	- **The live run view** at `$API/runs/<run id>` shows the team, a running timer, LLM calls and tokens per model,
2121	  the cost so far, and the score once the answer is in. Its timer ticks every second and the rest refreshes every
2122	  two seconds; it is what the projector shows.
2123	- **Your agent's screen:** run it on your laptop with a visible browser, or in our sandbox, whose desktop we can
2124	  show.
2125	- **Prepare:** a one-line command that starts your agent, such as `atira test-run ./my-agent` (it opens the run
2126	  page), a reliable network, and a fallback recording.
2127	
2128	---

result.output:
# Atira starter kit

A minimal starting point, not an agent. It does the platform plumbing: it reads the run, attaches to the run's
browsers and shows how to call the free hosted models. Then it stops at `solve()` in `agent.py`, the place for your
agent. Out of the box it exits without an answer.

| File | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `run.py` | The run contract: reads the run (`load_run`) and submits an API answer (`submit_answer`) |
| `browsers.py` | Attaches to the run's browsers over CDP and gets a page (`connect`); locally it starts a Chromium |
| `models.py` | One call to each hosted model: `ask_qwen` (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next) and `ask_clef` (Cloudflare Clef) |
| `agent.py` | The entry point: reads the run, connects browser 1, calls `solve(task, page)` and submits what it returns |
| `agent.json` | How the sandbox installs (`uv sync`, the versions in `uv.lock`) and runs it; it waits for the hosted `qwen` |
| `tests/` | The plumbing against fakes |

## Your agent goes in `solve()`

`solve(task, page)` gets the run and a Playwright page in browser 1:

- `task["brief"]`: the task and its rules;
- `task["access"]`: each website's `siteId`, `url` and `credentials`;
- `task["submission"]`: where the answer goes, `{"kind": "api", "url": ...}` or `{"kind": "site", "url": ...}`;
- `task["answer_schema"]`: the JSON Schema of the answer.

For an `api` submission, return the answer and `main()` submits it: `202` is accepted and final, `400` lists the
issues to fix. For a `site` submission, enter the answer on that website yourself and return `None`. Reading pages,
acting on them and working out the answer are yours to build.

Mind the clock: a scored run has 20 minutes, and `run.seconds_left(task)` says how many seconds are left. Every part
of the answer scores on its own, so submit your best answer about a minute before the end rather than keep
searching; an answer that comes too late scores 0.

More browsers: set `"browsers": 2` (up to 4) in `agent.json`, then `await browsers.connect(playwright, 1)` attaches
to browser 2.

## The hosted models in short

Both are free and need no key of yours: runs get the variables, and locally `atira scout --env` sets them, pointed
at `atira models proxy`.

```python
import models

text = await models.ask_qwen("Which button submits this form? ...")          # QWEN_BASE_URL, QWEN_API_KEY
yes = await models.ask_clef({"page": page_text}, "Is this the current revision?")  # CLEF_BASE_URL, CLEF_API_KEY
```

`models.qwen()` is an OpenAI SDK client, for tool calls, images and everything else. Clef is set only where the
platform hosts it; if your agent relies on it, list `"models": ["qwen", "clef"]` in `agent.json` so the run waits for
it to warm up. Another provider works with your own key through the run's metering proxy:
`$API/docs/run-contract.md#llm-calls`.

## Run it locally

You need [uv](https://docs.astral.sh/uv/getting-started/installation/) (open a new terminal after installing it, so
it is on your PATH) and the Atira CLI, signed in once with `atira login`.

Terminal 1: start the free models and leave it open.

```sh
atira models proxy
```

Terminal 2, in this folder:

```sh
uv sync && uv run playwright install chromium
eval "$(atira scout --env)"     # the scouting logins, and the model variables pointed at that proxy
uv run --no-sync python agent.py
```

In PowerShell on Windows, Terminal 2:

```powershell
uv sync; uv run playwright install chromium
atira scout --env | Out-String | Invoke-Expression    # the same exports
uv run --no-sync python agent.py
```

A Chromium window opens (`HEADLESS=1` hides it). Nothing done with the scouting logins counts, and locally an answer
is printed, never submitted. If `atira` says `Unknown command: models`, run `atira upgrade`.

## Test-run it, then submit it

```sh
atira test-run .   # the sandbox, exactly like a scored run, on the public dataset; opens the run page live
atira submit .     # reviewed, then run once and scored for the leaderboard
```

| `CHALLENGE_API_URL`, `CHALLENGE_RUN_TOKEN` | runs | the run, at `/v1/runs/current` |

| `CDP_URL`, `CDP_URLS` | runs | the sandbox's browsers; locally the kit starts its own Chromium |
| `QWEN_BASE_URL`, `QWEN_API_KEY` | runs, `atira scout --env` | the hosted Qwen |
